properties.statement:
A DANGLING `node_ref` PROPERTY IS REPORTED ONLY WHEN THE NODE CARRYING IT IS ALSO EDGELESS, SO A WELL-CONNECTED NODE POINTING AT NOTHING IS SILENT. Measured 2026-08-29 on reflow2's own graph, on the nine dangling `TemporalFact.subject_id` references that #366 identified and deliberately left for 'detection over the graph as it stands'.

THE MECHANISM IS IN THE FINDING'S OWN WORDS, so this is textual rather than inferred. `orphan_node` reports: 'points at nothing that exists — its subject/target id resolves to no node AND IT CARRIES NO EDGE EITHER, so the record is about something the design no longer has.' The conjunction is the defect. Dangling-reference detection is not a rule; it is a side effect of the orphan rule, and it inherits that rule's precondition.

THE MEASUREMENT, and the correlation is exact:

    edges on the fact   dangling target          reported by detect_defects?
    2                   cap:thin-install         NO
    1                   prj:reflow2              NO
    0  (x7)             the other seven          YES, all seven

So 7 of 9 surfaced and 2 did not — 22% invisible — and the two invisible ones are exactly the two that were attached to something. `detect_defects` returned 62 findings in that same run and neither was among them.

⚠️ WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A PLAIN ABSENCE: the rule LOOKS like it covers dangling references, and on this graph it covered 78% of them. A reader checking whether the class is detected finds seven examples of it being detected. The failure is invisible in exactly the way a partial detector always is — it produces evidence of working.

⭐ AND THE BIAS RUNS THE WRONG WAY. An edgeless node is by construction the LEAST consequential one to have a bad pointer, because nothing else reaches it. A node with edges is embedded in the design, so its pointer is read by more paths — and that is precisely the one this misses. The detector is most reliable where it matters least.

🛑 SCOPE, so this is not read wider than it is: measured on ONE property (`TemporalFact.subject_id`) on ONE graph. `node_ref` is a schema flag and other types may declare it; whether they do, and whether any of those carry dangling values, was NOT measured. The `create_node` guard shipped in #366 stops NEW bad values on any `node_ref` property, so this concerns only values written before that guard, or broken later by a rename — which is the residue #366 named as needing a different fix.

WHAT WOULD CLOSE IT: a rule that walks every property declared `node_ref` and reports an unresolvable value on its own terms, independent of the node's degree. The write-side guard already knows which properties those are.
